**Frame Format** The data link layer protocol packages the data passed down from the network layer in a protocol data unit called a frame. A *frame* consists of a header and a footer generated by the data link protocol, with the network layer data as the payload loaded in.

**Addressing** Every network interface adapter has a unique 6-byte identifier assigned to it by the manufacturer called a *media access control (MAC) address*. Data link layer use these addresses in their headers to identify the sender and recipient of each packet.

**Protocol Identification** Data link layer headers include a code that indicates which network layer protocol generated the data in each packet. This enables the data layer protocol on the receiving system to pass incoming traffic to the correct network layer process.

**Error Detection** The frame footer contains the result of a cyclic redundancy check (CRC) calculation performed on the frame data payload by the sending system. The receiving system performs the same calculation, and if the results do not match, disc the packet.

**Media Access Control (MAC)** When a LAN has devices connected to a shared network medium, the data link layer uses a media access mechanism to prevent two devices from transmitting simultaneously and causing a data collision.

**Physical Layer Specifications** The data link layer protocol also includes specifications for the physical layer options decoupled with the protocol.

Most called LANs run the Ethernet protocol at the data link layer, the actual name for which is IEEE 802.3, after the standards published by the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers. The functions just listed are all implemented as part of the Ethernet frame.

# Layer 3: The Network Layer

The protocols running at the physical and data link layers of the OSI model are dedicated to local network communications only. For example, Ethernet is capable of transmitting frames to another computer or router on the LAN; it is not concerned with the delivery of data to its final destination. That is the responsibility of the network layer protocol.

Network layer devices routers connect individual networks together, forming an *internetwork*, or network of networks. A *router* is an intermediate system that only processes incoming packets as high as the network layer, as shown in Figure 1.2.
